title: Brutalism vs Neo-Brutalism
lede: The common claim is that neo-brutalism is brutalism with rounded corners. In this gallery that is simply wrong: both keep every corner square. What actually changed is the palette and the shadow.
verdict: Brutalism is one accent on paper. Neo-brutalism is five candy fills on cream, with a deeper shadow stack — same skeleton, completely different temperature.
brief: Compare the two stylesheets and the structure is nearly identical: 3px black borders, hard offset shadows with zero blur, no gradients, no border radius anywhere. Both refuse the same things.

The difference is in two declarations. Brutalism keeps a single acid yellow against black and white, and its shadow tops out at 6px. Neo-brutalism introduces five tints — butter, mint, lilac, peach, cream — and pushes the stack to 8px, so each card looks like a sticker peeled off a sheet rather than a block printed on paper.

whenA: You need one loud surface in an otherwise quiet page — a single acid panel reads as a statement
The content is editorial and the type should feel slightly wrong on purpose
The page has very few cards; a broad palette with three cards looks accidental rather than playful
whenB: The page is a grid of many items and colour is how you differentiate them
The audience is consumer or creative, where candy tints read as energy rather than as a warning
You want each card to feel individually placed, which deeper shadows and multiple fills achieve
promptDelta: Both prompts start with the same sentence about hard black borders and zero-blur offset shadows, so the model will produce a similar skeleton either way. The steering happens in the palette clause: name one accent and the ban on other colours for brutalism; name five specific tints and a cream ground for neo-brutalism. Also state the radius explicitly — a model asked for neo-brutalism will add 8px corners by default because that is what most blog posts describe, and it will not look like this page.
